speaker_role: former admissions officer (almost 20 years in college admissions), now independent counselor/course creator
commercial_incentive: Promotes his own paid parents course on his website multiple times
key_insights: Defines ED as binding, EA as non-binding with decision due by ~May 1, and REA as non-binding but restricts applying early elsewhere except in-state publics
Early applicants are typically admitted at higher rates, and some schools fill 50-60%+ of their class from early rounds, especially ED
The ED agreement is signed by student, parent, and counselor and is described as ethically (not legally) binding
Breaking an ED agreement to keep other applications open can cause colleges to independently rescind admission, and may create reputational risk for future applicants from that high school
The only widely accepted reason to break an ED agreement is inadequate need-based financial aid after appealing; relying on a hoped-for merit scholarship is not a valid reason to apply ED
Recommends running the net price calculator before applying ED, and appealing at the financial aid office with those figures if the actual award falls short
ED2 exists at some schools with a ~January 1 deadline and mid-February decisions, letting a student who is deferred/rejected from ED1 apply to a second-choice binding program for an admissions boost
States the ED admit-rate boost can be double or triple the regular decision rate, but cautions that overall admit-rate comparisons don't capture the full picture ("admissions math")
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker says early applications are typically due in November with decisions by mid-December
Speaker says some institutions fill about 50-60%+ of their class from early applicants
Speaker says ED2 deadline is around January 1 with decisions by mid-February
Speaker says ED admit rates can be double or triple regular decision admit rates
notable_or_distinctive: Gives a concrete first-person anecdote of a student who tried to keep other applications open after ED admission, leading two institutions to independently rescind the offers.
reliability_notes: Presented as first-hand admissions experience with plausible specifics, but exact rescission/boost figures are anecdotal and not independently verifiable; video ends with a sales pitch for the speaker's paid course.
